topic: The Taum Sauk Upper Reservoir failure (December 14, 2005) — the control-system disaster: known-broken sensors, a computer that kept pumping into a full reservoir, and a fail-safe set above the top of the wall

primary_source.title: Taum Sauk Upper Dam Breach, FERC No. 2277 — Technical Reasons for the Breach of December 14, 2005 (Independent Panel of Consultants forensic report)
primary_source.authors: Paul C. Rizzo Associates / Independent Panel of Consultants (FERC-commissioned)

companion.title: FERC Staff Report — Taum Sauk Investigation (Division of Dam Safety and Inspections)

deep_extraction.claim: The parapet wall's LOWEST point had settled to Elev. 1597; the Hi-Hi Warrick emergency-shutdown probe was set at Elev. 1597.70 — 0.7 ft ABOVE the lowest point of the wall. Water physically overtopped the dam before the emergency stop could ever trigger.

The pressure transducers were reading ~4.2 ft LOW: penstock vs transducer comparison shows 12/13/05 5:50 readings of 1595.88 (penstock) vs 1591.68 (transducer); at 5:15 on 12/14 the transducers indicated 1593.70 while water was going over the 1597 wall.

The replacement level-sensing system (installed Nov 2004) was NOT anchored to the concrete face of the reservoir; the HDPE conduits housing the transducers moved, and protective pipe base plates were found unanchored with a guy cable loose after the breach.

On September 27, 2005 a 0.4 ft software offset was added to the transducer readings IN THE PLC CODE in response to visual observations disagreeing with the instruments — a software patch over a physical sensor failure. Transducer TX1 was removed from service the same day, making the remaining system MORE sensitive to temperature-induced error.

September 25, 2005 near-miss (two days after Hurricane Rita rains): workers witnessed overtopping described as 'Niagara Falls at the Northwest corner of the reservoir'; units were immediately put on generate mode to lower the reservoir. Documented in a 9/27/2005 internal email.

Internal email dated October 7, 2005: 'The Hi and Hi-Hi Warrick probes are 7" and 4" from the top of the wall respectively. So if on 9-27 the level was 4" below the wall the Hi level Warrick should have picked up.' And: 'If you want to lower the Hi level probes we can do that but I think we chose the levels...' — Ameren discussed and declined lowering the fail-safe setpoints ten weeks before the breach.

December 14, 2005 sequence: both units pumping in the early morning; at 04:39 Unit #2 shut down automatically at an INDICATED level of Elev. 1591.6; at 05:15 Unit #1 was shut down MANUALLY by the Bagnell Dam control center operator on instructions from the St. Louis control center — reservoir data indicate pumping stopped at 5:15 AM with the initial breach forming at approximately the same time.

Complete evacuation of the 4,350 acre-ft upper reservoir occurred within about 25 minutes of the initial breach; the flow passed down Proffit Mountain into the East Fork of the Black River through the State Park.
deep_extraction.cite: IPOC pp. 5, 17; FERC pp. 7, 138 (FERC uses ~4,300 acre-feet)

deep_extraction.claim: The parapet wall had experienced considerable deformation and settlement beginning with the FIRST FILLING of the reservoir (1963); the staff gage was affixed to the parapet wall and settled about one foot WITH the wall — AmerenUE believes the reservoir was actually operating at 1595 ft when indicating 1596 ft.

Panel 72 was the LOW POINT of the parapet wall; in an interview, plant superintendent Richard Cooper reported seeing wet spots on the downstream side of the parapet wall at the low point during a pre-breach morning visit.

The Emergency Action Plan notification: park superintendent Jerry Toops was ON the notification list; the call to the Toops house went unanswered — emergency personnel arriving on scene found the Toops house destroyed.

Control architecture: two Allen-Bradley PLCs (the Common PLC and the Upper Reservoir PLC, programmed with Rockwell RSLogix tooling) with a WonderWare Operator Interface for level indication, alarming, and data acquisition — installed in the 2004 upgrade.

The Warrick probe wiring: LO-LO and HI-HI were wired to alarm AND hard-stop the units, but the LO and HI probes would NOT generate an alarm — and the PLC historian would NOT even record in the logs that water had touched them. The intermediate warnings were silent and invisible by configuration.

Emergency preparedness: the last functional EAP exercise at Taum Sauk was May 1998 — seven years before the breach; the next was scheduled for 2008 (the licensee alternated exercises between its Osage and Taum Sauk projects).

Cooper's wet-spots account (nuance): he did not witness waves exceeding the wall; the wet spots at Panel 72 (the parapet low point) were possibly spray from waves — the observation that SHOULD have been a red flag was explainable-away in the moment.

timeline_events.event: Taum Sauk pumped-storage plant enters service: upper reservoir on Proffit Mountain (a rockfill dike with concrete parapet, NO emergency spillway), lower reservoir on the East Fork Black River; settlement of the parapet begins with first filling (IPOC p. 11).

New water-level instrumentation installed: pressure transducers in HDPE conduits NOT anchored to the liner, plus five Warrick conductivity probes (commissioned fall 2004) as backup shutdown (IPOC pp. 8, 15).
Near-miss overtopping after Hurricane Rita rains: 'Niagara Falls at the Northwest corner' witnessed by workers; units manually switched to generate to save the dam (IPOC p. 55).
Instead of a physical repair: a 0.4 ft software offset is coded into the PLC; transducer TX1 removed from service; internal email documents the near-miss (IPOC pp. 14, 21-22).
Internal email notes the shutdown probes sit 7 and 4 inches from the top of the wall and that on 9/27 the Hi probe 'should have picked up'; lowering the probes is discussed and deferred (IPOC p. 25).
Employees observe movement of the HDPE conduits housing the transducers; gauge disagreement continues; plant keeps operating on remote control from St. Louis (IPOC p. 8; web claims).
Unit #2 shuts down automatically at an INDICATED Elev. 1591.6 — the real level is ~4 ft higher; pumping continues on Unit #1 into a reservoir that is already at the wall (IPOC p. 16).

Water pours over the settled northwest parapet section; the rockfill dike erodes from the outside; at 05:15 Unit #1 is shut down MANUALLY from Bagnell Dam on St. Louis instructions — the breach is already forming (IPOC pp. 16-17).

The dike breaches ~656 ft wide; ~4,350 acre-ft (~1.4 billion gallons) evacuates in ~25 minutes down Proffit Mountain into Johnson's Shut-Ins State Park and the East Fork Black River (IPOC pp. 5, 17; damfailures.org).

The flood wave hits the park superintendent's home: the house fills in seconds; all five members of the Toops family are swept ~1/4 mile and survive with hypothermia; 5-year-old Tanner is resuscitated over two hours and requires skin grafts from rewarming burns (Deseret News 12/26/2005; MBC Pathway 2020 retrospective).
The EAP contact list is completed by plant staff; the call to the Toops house — on the notification list — goes unanswered; responders find the house destroyed (FERC pp. 133-134).
Within two weeks Ameren publicly attributes the failure to the automated instruments overpumping the reservoir and a backup system that failed to catch it (Deseret News/AP).
Johnson's Shut-Ins State Park rebuilt over ~4 years with phased reopenings from 2007 (STLPR).

FERC levies a $15 million civil penalty — the largest dam-safety penalty in FERC history at the time; Ameren settles with Missouri public entities for ~$180 million; the upper reservoir is rebuilt as a roller-compacted-concrete dam (online 2010, ~$490 million) (STLPR; web claims — penalty split needs a page-cited check against the consent agreement).

misconceptions.myth: It was a dam failure — an old dam finally gave out
misconceptions.reality: The dam failed because the CONTROL SYSTEM kept pumping: sensors under-read by 4 ft, the software got an offset patch instead of a repair, and the emergency probes were set above the wall's settled low point

misconceptions.myth: Nobody died, so it wasn't serious
misconceptions.reality: A family of five including a 7-month-old was swept a quarter mile in near-freezing pre-dawn water; a 5-year-old was clinically resuscitated over two hours. The zero-fatality outcome was luck measured in inches and minutes
Operators watched it nearly happen 80 days earlier ('Niagara Falls'), emailed that overtopping was 'an absolute NO-NO', discussed lowering the probes, and kept pumping

misconceptions.myth: Someone at the plant fell asleep
misconceptions.reality: Nobody was at the plant — it was run by remote control from St. Louis; the last-ditch manual stop came from ANOTHER dam's control room as the breach formed

audience_insights.knowledge_level: General audience knows dams can fail (Oroville, Teton footage familiarity); almost nobody knows pumped storage, and the sensor/PLC chain is fresh material. The Practical Engineering audience segment knows the mechanics but not the paper trail or the family story.

angles_discovered.angle: THE FAIL-SAFE WAS ABOVE THE WALL
angles_discovered.note: One sentence carries the whole disaster: the emergency stop was set 0.7 ft above the settled low point of the parapet. The wall let go before the machine was allowed to notice. Everything else is corollary.

angles_discovered.angle: The software patch over the physical failure
angles_discovered.note: Sept 27: instead of re-anchoring the conduits, a 0.4 ft offset went into the PLC code. Our genre's thesis in miniature: patching the reading instead of the reality.
The EAP worked exactly as written — and the first call on the list rang in a house that no longer existed. Cold open or closing beat.

angles_discovered.angle: The measuring stick sank with the wall
angles_discovered.note: The staff gage was bolted to the parapet and settled with it — even the humans' visual check was calibrated to a sinking reference. Nothing in the loop touched reality.

modern_relevance.note: Sensor-trust failures with software patches over physical faults recur: Boeing 737 MAX MCAS (single-AoA-sensor authority), the 2021 Oldsmar water-treatment remote-access scare, alarm-fatigue findings in process industries (Texas City). Pumped storage is ALSO newly topical as grid-battery infrastructure for renewables — the same plant type being built worldwide today. Frame: the machines we trust to watch the water are only as honest as their worst sensor.
hooks: MCAS parallel: one lying sensor, software authority, no cross-check
grid-storage boom: we are building many more Taum Sauks
